extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, historians, and policymakers interested in democratic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and evaluative propositions from Alexis de Tocqueville's discussion of equality, public opinion, revolutions, and the character of democratic armies. The page is an interpretive political-philosophical text, not a procedural rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracies favor gradual change, not revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Americans constantly modify or abrogate some of their laws, they by no means display revolutionary passions; they love change, but they dread revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic societies 'bestir themselves within certain limits' and 'carefully abstain from touching what is fundamental.' They check and calm themselves when public excitement grows; the majority display little inclination for principles that threaten property. Revolutionary theories are less favorably viewed because they would require sudden change in property and persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality tends to produce intellectual stability of major principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When once an opinion has spread over the country and struck root there, it would seem that no power on earth is strong enough to eradicate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the United States general principles in religion, philosophy, morality, and politics 'do not vary, or at least are only modified by a hidden and often an imperceptible process.' Change of deep beliefs requires repeated experience rather than speech or writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic minds are active in secondary variation but resistant to new foundational principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The human mind is in constant agitation; it is engaged in infinitely varying the consequences of known principles, rather than in seeking for new principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion is 'one of rapid circumvolution' — many small continual movements altering consequences and practices, not sudden adoption of new fundamental doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion in democracies exerts overwhelming social pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever social conditions are equal, public opinion presses with enormous weight upon the mind of each individual; it surrounds, directs, and oppresses him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because men are similar and stand alone, they 'mistrust' themselves when assailed by the majority; public disapprobation suffices where laws are unnecessary. This social force makes it extremely difficult to profess what the majority condemn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of majority opinion often happens silently and slowly
rubrics_metrics.description: Time, events, or the unaided individual action of the mind will sometimes undermine or destroy an opinion, without any outward sign of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Followers 'one by one noiselessly secede' and the majority may cease to believe while still professing the old opinion; silence of dissenters produces a persistent phantom of public opinion that chills innovators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great intellectual revolutions most likely in intermediate social structures
rubrics_metrics.description: A state favorable to great revolutions of the mind occurs somewhere between complete equality and absolute separation of ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rigid caste systems imagination 'slumbers.' Full equality produces isolated individuals; the intermediate period—where conditions are neither fixed nor fully equal—permits a few to modify convictions of many and allows great reformers to arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic nations are naturally desirous of peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The ever-increasing numbers of men of property—lovers of peace, the growth of personal wealth which war so rapidly consumes, the mildness of manners... all these causes concur to quench the military spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because equality increases the number of property-holders and private pursuits, democratic societies prefer peace as conducive to industry and personal advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic armies are uniquely prone to desire war
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic armies all the soldiers may become officers, which makes the desire of promotion general... All the ambitious spirits of a democratic army are consequently ardently desirous of war, because war makes vacancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality makes military honors accessible and important for social status; limited commissions plus universal ambition render officers and soldiers disposed toward conflict to advance their careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between pacific populace and warlike army creates special dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all nations those most fond of peace are democratic nations; and of all armies those most ardently desirous of war are democratic armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrast leads to risks: when the nation scorns the military profession the army becomes restive and less esteemed, and soldiers/officers may seek hostilities or revolutions to gain influence. A large army among an unwarlike people endangers the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: War tends to concentrate civil power and risks gradual despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: No protracted war can fail to endanger the freedom of a democratic country. War... must almost compulsorily concentrate the direction of all men and the management of all things in the hands of the administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when war does not produce immediate military rule, it prepares citizens for strong centralized government by habit and administration, making it a chief avenue to the destruction of liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanding the army is not a cure for military ambition in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase the army may produce a lasting effect in an aristocratic community... But nothing is gained by increasing the army amongst a democratic people, because the number of aspirants always rises in exactly the same ratio as the army itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating more commissions only temporarily relieves ambition; it multiplies claimants and fuels perpetual desire for promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The remedy to army vices lies in national civic culture, not military reform alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy for the vices of the army is not to be found in the army itself, but in the country... Teach but the citizens to be educated, orderly, firm, and free, the soldiers will be disciplined and obedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fostering peaceful, disciplined civic habits and respect for rights across society diffuses into the army; laws that repress army turbulence at the cost of national freedom are counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory service and transient enlistment shape democratic armies' composition
rubrics_metrics.description: When military service is compulsory, the burden is indiscriminately and equally borne by the whole community... each of them remains but for a few years on active duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because soldiers serve briefly and return to civil life, private soldiers retain civilian habits and can be carriers of the nation's love of freedom into the army; officers, by contrast, may sever ties and develop distinct, more warlike interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers in democracies tend to form a distinct, more ambitious military caste
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst democratic nations the man who becomes an officer severs all the ties which bound him to civil life... his true country is the army, since he owes all he has to the rank he has attained in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers' social position depends on military rank, making them more invested in the army's success and more inclined toward war or revolution than the general populace; this difference amplifies civil-military tension.
